opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that AI didn't so much create new problems as take the problems we already had and turn the dial up to eleven.

If you go back ten years, data center networking was already wrestling with some hard issues. You had huge numbers of servers that needed to talk to each other, traffic patterns that were very bursty and hard to predict, and the classic problem of incast, where lots of senders all try to talk to one receiver at the same moment, queues overflow, packets get dropped, and latency spikes. We built a lot of machinery to cope with that: better congestion control, ECN, multipath topologies like Clos networks, and so on. For most cloud workloads, that was good enough, because the traffic was a mix of lots of independent things and statistical multiplexing smoothed things out.

What large-scale AI training does is remove that smoothing. A training job is essentially one enormous, tightly synchronized program running across tens of thousands or even hundreds of thousands of GPUs. At the end of each step, everybody needs to exchange gradients, all at once, in collective operations like all-reduce. So instead of lots of uncorrelated flows, you get massive, synchronized bursts where every node hits the network at the same instant. And crucially, the whole job moves at the speed of the slowest participant. If one flow gets unlucky, hits a congested link, loses a packet and waits for a retransmit timeout, then thousands of extremely expensive GPUs sit there idle waiting for it. Tail latency stops being a nuisance and becomes the thing that determines your efficiency.

The second change is the sheer scale and the economics. The network used to be a relatively modest fraction of the cost of a data center. Now you're connecting accelerators that are each enormously expensive, so any inefficiency in the network gets multiplied by the cost of all that idle compute. That justifies engineering effort that wouldn't have made sense before.

And third, the traditional approach the industry leaned on for this kind of high-performance traffic, RDMA over Converged Ethernet, was designed assuming a lossless network. You use priority flow control to avoid dropping packets, and that works at modest scale, but as you scale up you start running into head-of-line blocking, congestion spreading, even deadlocks. Plus, those protocols tend to send each flow down a single path, so with ECMP hashing you get collisions where a few big flows land on the same link while other links sit idle. Load balancing becomes a real problem when your flows are few and enormous, rather than many and small.

So a lot of the work I've been involved in, and that the wider community has been doing, for example through efforts like Ultra Ethernet, is rethinking the transport layer from first principles for this world. Things like spraying packets across all available paths rather than pinning a flow to one path, so you use the whole fabric evenly. Tolerating out-of-order delivery so spraying is actually workable. Making loss cheap to recover from rather than trying to prevent it at all costs, for instance trimming packets to just their headers when queues fill, so the receiver knows immediately what's missing and can ask for it without waiting for a timeout. And designing congestion control that reacts in about a round-trip time, because at these speeds, if you wait longer, the burst is already over.

A lot of those ideas weren't new. Some of them we were exploring in research a decade ago with things like multipath TCP and NDP. But at the time the pain wasn't severe enough to justify changing the hardware and the whole stack. AI changed that calculus. Suddenly the problems that were academic became the bottleneck on some of the most expensive computers ever built, and that's made the industry willing to rethink things it had been reluctant to touch for a long time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that AI didn't create new networking problems so much as it took problems we already had and turned the dial all the way up.

If you think about what a conventional data center looked like, you had lots of fairly independent workloads. A web request comes in, it touches a few machines, it goes out. There's a lot of statistical multiplexing, and the network was designed around that. You could tolerate some loss, you could tolerate some latency variance, because any individual flow was a small part of the whole and TCP would sort it out.

AI training is almost the opposite of that. You have thousands of GPUs that are effectively working on one computation, and they synchronize constantly. Every few milliseconds you have an all-reduce or an all-to-all where everyone has to exchange data with everyone, and the whole thing can't proceed until the slowest piece arrives. So the tail latency, which was always something we cared about, suddenly becomes the whole game. One congested link, one retransmission timeout, and you've got tens of millions of dollars of hardware sitting idle waiting.

The second thing is the traffic itself. These are very large, very synchronized flows. They start together, they're long, and they're bursty in lockstep. That's precisely the pattern that defeats the load balancing we've relied on. ECMP works nicely when you have lots of small flows and the hash spreads them out. When you've got a handful of elephant flows all starting at once, the hash collisions are brutal, and you end up with some links at a hundred percent and others sitting empty. So the industry has had to go back and look seriously at packet spraying, at adaptive routing, at things that people like me were arguing for a decade ago and which were considered too exotic at the time.

And then there's the loss question. The GPU vendors came at this from the InfiniBand world, where the assumption is a lossless fabric. Ethernet people have spent years trying to bolt losslessness on with priority flow control, and PFC has all these pathologies, head-of-line blocking, deadlocks, congestion spreading. My own view has always been that you're better off making the transport handle loss and congestion intelligently rather than trying to pretend the network is perfect. That's a big part of what we were doing with NDP, and it's a lot of what's going on now with things like the Ultra Ethernet work, trying to design a transport that's actually built for this traffic rather than retrofitted.

So in short, the scale got bigger, the margin for error got smaller, and a lot of old debates that were somewhat academic suddenly had very real money attached to them.

astra-6.text:
I think AI has taken challenges that were already there and turned the dial up quite dramatically. A data center network has always had to connect a large number of machines with high bandwidth, and deal with traffic arriving in bursts. But with AI training, you have a very large number of accelerators working together on what is essentially one computation.

Those accelerators need to exchange information, and at various points they have to wait for one another. So it’s not enough for the network to perform well on average. If one part of that communication is slow, you can end up with a lot of very expensive hardware sitting idle.

That changes the economics as well as the engineering. You need much more bandwidth, but you also need to use it efficiently and deliver fairly predictable performance. Problems like congestion, load balancing, and the slowest transfer holding everything else up were already familiar in data centers. AI makes the consequences of those problems much greater.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI has taken a set of problems that data centers already had and made them much more acute. You were already trying to connect large numbers of machines with high bandwidth and low latency. But with distributed training, those machines are working together on one computation, so the network becomes part of the computer in a very direct way.

That changes the cost of a delay. If one transfer is slow, it can hold up a whole group of very expensive accelerators. So you care about bandwidth, but you also care about how consistently you can deliver it—how you handle congestion, how you spread traffic across paths, and what happens when something fails.

And the traffic can be quite coordinated. Lots of machines reach the same stage of a computation and need to communicate at roughly the same time. So AI hasn’t invented the networking challenges, but it has pushed them to a scale and an intensity where things that were tolerable inefficiencies become very expensive bottlenecks.
